tldr: This paper presents ADEPT, a reinforcement learning framework that pre-trains multi-fingered hands on generic object reposing and then adapts them to downstream contact-rich tasks through carefully designed post-training to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Operating directly from raw RGB camera images and fingertip tactile sensors without human demonstrations or external fixtures, it achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, completing challenging peg insertion and plate racking tasks at human-level speed (5–10 seconds).
hero_caption: Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of policies learned by ADEPT across complex manipulation sequences. Top: A 23-DoF Kuka-Allegro performs plate racking (picking, flipping, regrasping, and insertion) using RGB cameras alone. Bottom: A 29-DoF Flexiv-Sharpa accomplishes the challenging FMB peg insertion using cameras and five vision-based fingertip tactile sensors in a single, fluid motion.
overview:
Combining multi-fingered hands with robot arms holds great promise for human-like dexterous manipulation. However, high degrees of freedom (DoF) and complex contacts make discovering skills from scratch with reinforcement learning (RL) extremely difficult. Even with massively parallel GPU simulation, agents typically re-learn basic reaching, grasping, and lifting behaviors for each new task, limiting learning efficiency and generality.

To address this, the authors introduce the pre-training and post-training paradigm—widely successful in NLP and computer vision—into robotic manipulation. First, they pre-train foundational dexterity using RL on a generic reposing task involving 16 simple primitive object shapes, training the policy to lift and rotate them to target poses. However, directly fine-tuning this policy on downstream contact-rich tasks (such as peg insertion) using naive RL quickly destroys the pre-trained skills (catastrophic forgetting) due to observation space mismatches and inaccurate value function estimates.

The authors overcome this challenge with a structured post-training recipe combining behavior-cloning distillation, critic warm-up, and conservative on-policy PPO updates. Furthermore, they introduce a joint-space Geometric Fabric to safely exploit the robot's full kinematic dexterity, along with a two-stage distillation pipeline that transfers privileged teacher policies to student policies operating from raw camera images and tactile readings.

Validated across two distinct hardware embodiments—a 23-DoF Kuka-Allegro and a 29-DoF Flexiv-Sharpa—the framework achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. On the challenging FMB peg insertion task, which took 20–70 seconds with parallel grippers and external fixtures, ADEPT solves the task via in-hand regrasping in just 5–10 seconds, matching human-level speed and demonstrating that pre-training substantially accelerates the learning of contact-rich manipulation.
contributions: Proposed ADEPT, an RL framework that pre-trains foundational dexterity on generic object reposing and adapts it to downstream contact-rich tasks.

Developed a Cspace Geometric Fabric that mediates between the policy and the robot, opening the full joint space of high-DoF arm-hand systems without restricting them to low-dimensional PCA grasp spaces while avoiding collisions and joint limits.

Established a structured post-training recipe (actor distillation, critic warm-up, conservative PPO) to prevent skill degradation, paired with a two-stage distillation curriculum for progressive perception learning.

Demonstrated the first zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on challenging pick-reorient-insert tasks directly from raw visual and tactile observations, without human demonstrations, external fixtures, or explicit pose estimators.

sections.heading: Why keep learning multi-fingered dexterity from scratch?
sections.summary: Multi-fingered RL features large state-action spaces and intricate contacts, causing agents trained from scratch to waste time rediscovering basic grasps for every task. This work introduces ADEPT, a framework that pre-trains dexterity on generic reposing and adapts it downstream. A novel post-training recipe prevents skill collapse during naive fine-tuning, enabling zero-shot real-world deployment.
sections.details:
Robot arms equipped with multi-fingered hands face huge state-action spaces and intricate contacts, making it very difficult to discover useful skills from sparse rewards from scratch. Even with large-scale GPU simulation, agents repeatedly re-learn identical primitive skills—reaching, grasping, lifting, and reorienting—for every single task, yielding policies that fail to generalize across tasks.

The authors focus on the importance of the initialization point in policy parameter space. Pre-training on a diverse set of motor primitives places network weights in a favorable region. This allows downstream training to build upon existing capabilities rather than overwriting and destroying them.

ADEPT pre-trains foundational dexterity on generic object reposing tasks (lifting and placing objects at target positions and orientations) and post-trains these skills on downstream contact-rich tasks. While the pre-trained policy zero-shots the transport phase of downstream tasks, naive PPO fine-tuning rapidly degrades these skills due to observation discrepancies and value estimation errors. To prevent this collapse, the authors introduce a structured post-training procedure: behavior-cloning actor distillation, critic warm-up, and conservative on-policy PPO updates.

Privileged teacher policies are then distilled via a two-stage curriculum into student models that take raw RGB camera images and tactile inputs, enabling zero-shot transfer to real hardware. Evaluated on the hardest asymmetric peg insertions from the Functional Manipulation Benchmark (FMB) and plate racking, ADEPT finishes tasks in 5–10 seconds, compared to 20–70 seconds required by parallel-jaw grippers.

sections.heading: Lineage: Sim-to-real, RL pre-training, and geometric control
sections.summary: Prior works often tackled single-skill sim-to-real transfer or relied on pose estimators, leaving raw-perception multi-fingered manipulation largely unexplored. ADEPT bridges this gap by combining full-DoF control via Geometric Fabrics, stable post-training without explicit regularization penalties, and unified tactile representations.
sections.details:
Related work and the positioning of this paper span four main domains:

- Sim-to-Real Multi-Fingered Dexterity: Prior efforts used large-scale PPO and domain randomization for in-hand reorientation, but most relied on external object/target pose estimators or required human demonstrations as initializations. ADEPT transfers student policies that run directly on raw RGB images and fingertip tactile sensors without pose estimators or demonstrations.

- RL Pre-Training and Transfer: Past methods added regularization penalties like KL divergence or EWC to prevent forgetting during online adaptation, which often overly constrain high-DoF hands. ADEPT achieves stable adaptation without explicit penalty terms by combining imitation actor distillation, critic warm-up, and a significantly lowered actor learning rate.

- Geometric Fabrics for Policy Learning: Geometric Fabrics provide smooth, second-order controllers that natively encode collision and joint-limit avoidance. While prior methods like DextrAH restricted hand control to 5-dimensional PCA human-grasp synergies, ADEPT exposes the full joint configuration space (Cspace, 23–29 DoF) to the policy, enabling finely coordinated fingertip contact manipulation.

- Sim-to-Real Tactile Sensing: Due to the large reality gap in simulated contact forces, the framework adopts geometric penetration depth maps (TacMap) as a common representation and spatially conditions them with forward-kinematics fingertip positions via FiLM, following the SaTA approach.

sections.heading: A three-stage framework: From pre-training to real-world deployment
sections.summary: ADEPT consists of three stages: (1) generic reposing pre-training, (2) structured post-training, and (3) two-stage student distillation. At the low level, a Cspace Geometric Fabric guarantees safety while unlocking full joint dexterity.
sections.details:
The complete ADEPT pipeline consists of three core stages, as illustrated in Figure F2.

3.1 Problem Formulation
Arm-hand manipulation is framed as a discrete-time Markov Decision Process (MDP). The pre-training MDP ($\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{pre}}$) and downstream MDP ($\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{post}}$) share the same action space (joint position targets), but the downstream task introduces extra observations such as receptacle pose $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{rec}}$ and contact wrench $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{or}}$, alongside task-specific rewards.

3.2 Foundational Dexterity Pre-Training
The agent learns to lift 16 simple primitive shapes (cylinders, cuboids, spheres, cones) from a tabletop and repose them to random target 6D poses. Automatic Domain Randomization (ADR) gradually scales gravity from $0 \to -9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, while Population-Based Training (PBT) tunes PPO hyperparameters, allowing diverse grasping and in-hand reorientation strategies to emerge naturally.

3.3 Structured Post-Training for Downstream Tasks
Naive fine-tuning immediately collapses pre-trained skills due to observation shifts, reward function changes, and large gradient updates from inaccurate initial value estimates. ADEPT resolves this via three sequential steps:
- (1) BC Actor Distillation: Distills the actions of teacher $\pi_{\mathrm{pre}}$ into a new downstream actor $\pi_{\mathrm{post}}$ (which takes downstream observations) using supervised behavior cloning for 40k iterations.
- (2) Critic Warm-Up: Freezes the actor and trains only the new critic $V_{\mathrm{post}}$ on downstream task rewards for 20 iterations to calibrate value estimates.
- (3) Conservative PPO: Reduces the actor learning rate to 1/100th of its pre-training value ($10^{-3} \to 10^{-5}$) and tightens the PPO clip parameter to $\epsilon=0.05$ to keep updates close to the pre-trained distribution.

3.4 Teacher-to-Student Distillation
The privileged teacher is distilled into a student policy relying solely on deployable inputs (proprioception, stereo RGB, fingertip tactile maps). To avoid conflict between visual representation learning and policy optimization, a two-stage curriculum is used: Stage 1 trains the visual backbone from the reposing teacher using an auxiliary 3D bounding box loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}$) on the peg's 8 vertices; Stage 2 refines the entire policy using the downstream insertion teacher.

3.5 Cspace Geometric Fabrics
A Geometric Fabric sits between the RL policy and the robot. The policy outputs relative full-joint targets at 60 Hz. The fabric shapes these into smooth, second-order trajectories that respect joint limits and prevent self- and environment collisions, feeding them into a 1 kHz admittance controller.

sections.heading: Why does naive transfer fail? Real-world validation of superior dexterity
sections.summary: Simulation ablations explain why naive fine-tuning collapses immediately whereas ADEPT learns stably. Hardware experiments on two arm-hand platforms demonstrate successful peg insertion and plate racking, revealing that tactile feedback dramatically improves grasping confidence.
sections.details:
4.1 Simulation Experiments
- Generalization to Unseen Objects and Zero-Shot Transfer: Teachers pre-trained on just 16 primitive shapes reposed unseen objects from FMB and VisDex with success rates matching or exceeding training shapes. The pre-trained policy achieved over 50% zero-shot success on the transport phase (up to ADR level 35) of the FMB peg insertion task. However, performance dropped to 0% at the insertion contact phase (ADR 50), identifying ADR 20 as the optimal entry point for post-training.
- Comparison with Training from Scratch: Training from scratch failed to progress across most random seeds even after 9B steps. In contrast, ADEPT solved the downstream task with only 3B post-training steps on top of 8B pre-training steps. Crucially, pre-training costs are amortized across multiple downstream tasks.
- Why Does Naive Fine-Tuning Fail?: Ablation studies (Table 3) revealed the actor learning rate as the single most critical factor. At a learning rate of $10^{-3}$, performance collapsed to 0% across all seeds, even with KL penalties. Lowering the learning rate to $10^{-5}$, paired with critic warm-up (+17.6% success rate) and BC distillation (reducing adaptation time from 35.2 to 19.9 hours), proved essential.
- Natural Grasps and Novel Behaviors: While scratch policies produced unnatural fingertip bends, ADEPT retained natural, power-style grasps from pre-training. Furthermore, when handling large, flat plates (unseen during pre-training), the policy leveraged pre-trained reaching primitives to discover a novel 'flip-and-regrasp' behavior for upside-down plates.

4.2 Real-World Experiments
Evaluated on Kuka-Allegro (vision-only) and Flexiv-Sharpa (vision + tactile).
- Real-World Success Rates: Kuka-Allegro achieved 5/10 on the FMB star peg, 3/10 on the hardest round-corner asymmetric peg, and 6/10 on plate racking. The tactile-enabled Flexiv-Sharpa achieved 8/10 on the round-corner asymmetric peg.
- Critical Role of Tactile Sensing: On Flexiv-Sharpa, vision-only students achieved only 3/10, whereas adding fingertip tactile sensing raised success to 8/10. Without tactile feedback, the student lacked confidence in grasp security, entering repetitive release-regrasp loops. Tactile feedback confirmed contact, stabilizing pick-and-flip success to 100%.
- Human-Level Speed: ADEPT executes pick, mid-air reorientation, and insertion as a single, fluid motion in 5–10 seconds. This is 2–14 times faster than original FMB baseline benchmarks (20–70 seconds using parallel grippers and fixtures).

sections.heading: Sensory challenges under occlusion and fingertip shape limitations
sections.summary: While real-world execution closely mirrors simulation, visual pose errors caused by hand and arm occlusions remain the primary mode of failure. In addition, hard, rounded fingertips present physical stability challenges on slippery objects.
sections.details:
Although real-world executions closely replicated simulation behaviors, the primary bottleneck on hardware was perception rather than control.

When manipulating asymmetric pegs, the robot's own hand and fingers frequently occluded the object. This caused errors in image-based pose predictions and resulted in missed insertions. While tactile sensing on the Flexiv-Sharpa resolved contact ambiguities, building occlusion-robust, object-centric visual representations remains an open challenge.

From a hardware perspective, the spherical, rigid fingertips of the Allegro hand create very small contact patches on curved peg surfaces. This occasionally caused slippage during high-acceleration arm motions. The authors suggest that adding wrist-mounted cameras and equipping more platforms with tactile sensors will be valuable next steps.

sections.heading: How pre-training dexterity unlocks the next frontier of robot learning
sections.summary: This study demonstrates that pre-training on generic reposing combined with structured post-training significantly accelerates and stabilizes multi-fingered RL. Expanding pre-training task distributions to bimanual manipulation, tool use, and cluttered scenes is an exciting next step.
sections.details:
This paper presented ADEPT, a reinforcement learning framework for high-DoF dexterous arm-hand systems. By acquiring foundational motor primitives through generic reposing pre-training and adapting them via structured post-training, it eliminates the need to reinvent basic grasping behaviors for every new downstream task.

Across two hardware setups (Kuka-Allegro and Flexiv-Sharpa), the framework solved long-horizon pick, reorient, transport, and insert tasks from raw visual and tactile streams at human-level speeds.

An important future milestone is expanding the pre-training task distribution. Promising directions include richer in-hand manipulation, tool use, obstacle-filled cluttered environments, and bimanual manipulation, exploring how far pre-trained dexterity can transfer to tasks that differ substantially from the pre-training distribution.

sections.heading: Appendix: Primitive shapes, reward formulations, and fabric mathematics
sections.summary: The appendix details the 16 primitive training shapes, reward formulations for reposing and downstream tasks, and mathematical derivations for the Cspace Geometric Fabric that ensures safe trajectories across the full joint space.
sections.details:
The appendix provides essential implementation details for reproducing and understanding the methodology:

- Pre-Training Objects and Rewards (Appendix A.1):
Pre-training utilizes 16 primitive shapes spanning cuboids, spheres, capsules, and cones (Figure F6). The reward function consists of an approach reward $r_r$, a goal-alignment reward $r_g$ based on 8-vertex bounding box distances, and a regularization term $r_b$ penalizing excessive finger curling. ADR schedules gradually increase gravity and pose tolerances.

- Post-Training Hyperparameters (Appendix A.3, D):
Key PPO differences between pre-training and downstream post-training include reducing the actor learning rate by a factor of 100 ($10^{-3} \to 10^{-5}$) and tightening the PPO clip ratio $\epsilon$ from 0.2 to 0.05 (Table 5). Furthermore, actor and critic network backbones are split from a shared architecture into independent networks, preventing downstream critic updates from destabilizing pre-trained actor features.

- Cspace Geometric Fabrics Formulation (Appendix B):
The system's equation of motion is defined as $\mathbf{M}_f(\mathbf{q}_f,\dot{\mathbf{q}}_f)\,\ddot{\mathbf{q}}_f + \mathbf{f}_f(\mathbf{q}_f,\dot{\mathbf{q}}_f) = \mathbf{f}_\pi(\mathbf{a})$. Geometric repulsive and damping forces across 31 collision spheres placed along robot links and finger phalanges are encoded into $\mathbf{f}_f$. Even if the policy outputs aggressive targets, the fabric layer modifies them into safe accelerations that avoid collisions and joint limits.

- Tactile Encoder and Spatial Integration via FiLM (Appendix H):
TacMap depth images and binary contact masks from the Flexiv-Sharpa's five fingertips are processed by a shared lightweight CNN. They are spatially conditioned via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) conditioned on Fourier features of 3D fingertip coordinates obtained from forward kinematics, providing the policy with clear spatial cues about where and which finger is contacting the object.

takeaways: In multi-fingered RL, generic object reposing (lifting and reorienting) serves as an exceptionally powerful foundational skill that significantly accelerates downstream tasks.
Catastrophic forgetting during downstream fine-tuning is effectively prevented not by explicit KL penalties, but by a 100x reduction in actor learning rate, BC distillation, and critic warm-up.
Using a Cspace Geometric Fabric preserves the full kinematic dexterity of high-DoF hands without falling back on low-dimensional PCA grasp synergies, while maintaining hardware safety.
Fingertip tactile sensing plays a decisive role in contact-rich real-world tasks by providing certainty about grasp success, eliminating unproductive regrasp loops.
limitations: Object pose predictions from RGB cameras are vulnerable to self-occlusions caused by the robot hand and arm, leading to occasional insertion failures.
Rigid, rounded fingertips (e.g., on the Allegro hand) provide very small contact patches on curved surfaces, which can lead to slippage during high-speed arm motions.
Tasks that diverge heavily from the reposing pre-training distribution (such as tool use or bimanual coordination) may not be fully covered by the current single-hand reposing pre-training scheme.
